title: Implement vector storage in Azure Managed Redis

questions.q: Your app has a 1,536-float NumPy embedding to store in a Redis hash for vector search. How should it be stored?

options.why: A text string isn't the binary format the index expects.
Correct. Redis stores hash vectors as binary blobs for efficiency.
The vector is one field holding bytes.

options.text: As a JSON array in a hash field
options.why: JSON arrays are for Redis JSON documents, not hash fields.

questions.hint: Redis Hash fields hold strings or bytes. Convert the array to raw bytes.
questions.explain: Convert NumPy arrays with tobytes() before storing them in a hash.

questions.q: Which dialect must you set for Redis vector queries?

options.why: Learn says vector queries need dialect 2.
Vector queries require dialect 2.
Correct. Use .dialect(2) for vector queries.
Learn specifies dialect 2.

questions.hint: Vector queries need a specific query dialect.
questions.explain: Query("*=>[KNN 5 @embedding $query_vec AS score]").dialect(2)

questions.q: You need the 3 nearest documents to a question, but only within the documentation category. Which query string is correct?

options.why: The KNN clause belongs after =>.
Correct. The filter goes before the vector search operator =>.
The filter must come before =>, not after the KNN clause.
VECTOR_RANGE takes a distance threshold, not a count, and this isn't the filter syntax.

questions.hint: Put the filter before the arrow and the KNN clause after it.
questions.explain: Hybrid queries filter first, then find the K nearest within the filtered set.

questions.q: A support bot must return every document within cosine distance 0.2 of the question, however many that is. Which query type fits?

options.why: Correct. Range queries return all vectors within the distance.

options.text: A KNN query with K set to 100
options.why: KNN returns a fixed number, not everything within a threshold.

options.text: A FLAT index queried with K = 1
options.why: FLAT is an algorithm; K = 1 returns one result.

options.text: A query with EF_RUNTIME set to 0.2
options.why: EF_RUNTIME is an exploration count, not a distance threshold.

questions.hint: "However many" means a distance cut-off, not a fixed count.
questions.explain: KNN = fixed count; VECTOR_RANGE = everything within a distance.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An index has `DIM 1536`, `DISTANCE_METRIC COSINE` and prefix `doc:`.

rows.text: Adding a hash with key doc:042 and an embedding field indexes it automatically.
rows.why: Redis indexes keys with the prefix automatically.

rows.text: A query with a 768-dimension vector returns approximate results.
rows.why: Dimension mismatches are rejected with an error.

rows.text: A score of 0.05 means the document is very similar to the query.
rows.why: Lower COSINE distance means more similar.

rows.text: Loading 1 million documents with individual hset calls is the fastest way to ingest.

questions.hint: Prefixed keys are indexed automatically. Query dimensions must match exactly.
questions.explain: Match DIM exactly, read scores as distances, and use pipelines for bulk loads.

questions.q: A team stores image embeddings and uses COSINE because "it's best for text". Results look odd. What does Learn recommend for image embeddings and spatial data?

options.why: Correct. L2 suits image embeddings and spatial data where magnitude matters.
The metric, not the algorithm, is the issue.
EF_RUNTIME tunes exploration, not the metric.
IP is only for pre-normalized embeddings.

questions.hint: COSINE suits text. Images and spatial data use a different metric.
questions.explain: COSINE for text, L2 for images and spatial data, IP for pre-normalized embeddings.

questions.q: HNSW queries are fast but sometimes miss clearly relevant documents. What should you adjust first?

options.text: Lower DIM to 768 in the index schema
options.why: DIM must match the model exactly.

options.text: Remove dialect(2) from the vector query
options.why: Vector queries need dialect 2.
Changing the metric would break semantic results for text.
Correct. Higher EF_RUNTIME explores more of the graph for better accuracy.

questions.hint: HNSW explores a limited part of the graph. One runtime setting widens the search.
questions.explain: EF_RUNTIME trades speed for accuracy per query.

questions.q: An ingestion script loads 500,000 documents with one hset call each, and throughput tops out at a few hundred writes per second. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Store the embeddings as JSON text strings instead of bytes
options.why: Text strings are larger and don't fix network round trips.

options.text: Batch the hset commands in a pipeline and call execute()
options.why: Correct. Pipelines batch commands into one round trip, which removes per-command network overhead.

options.text: Create a new index for every 10,000 documents
options.why: Many indexes complicate search and don't speed up writes.

options.text: Switch the index algorithm from HNSW to FLAT
options.why: The algorithm affects search, not how fast you can send writes.

questions.hint: Each command waits for a network round trip. How do you send many at once?
questions.explain: Individual hset commands are limited by network overhead to a few hundred per second. Pipelines batch many commands and send them in one round trip.

questions.q: What does the query string *=>[KNN 5 @embedding $query_vec AS score] do?

options.text: Searches only documents whose embedding field equals the query vector
options.why: KNN finds the nearest vectors, not exact matches.

options.text: Returns every document within a distance of 5 from the query vector
options.why: That's a range query. KNN returns a fixed number of results.

options.text: Searches all documents and returns the 5 nearest neighbors in the embedding field, with a score
options.why: Correct. * means no pre-filter, KNN 5 asks for five neighbors, and AS score names the distance.

options.text: Returns 5 random documents and scores them against the query
options.why: KNN ranks by distance. It doesn't pick at random.

questions.hint: Read it in parts: what the asterisk means, what KNN 5 asks for, and what AS names.
questions.explain: *=>[KNN 5 @embedding $query_vec AS score] searches all documents, finds 5 nearest neighbors in @embedding and returns their scores. Use .dialect(2), and pass the query vector as bytes.

questions.q: Your embedding model outputs pre-normalized vectors, and its documentation asks for inner product scoring. Which DISTANCE_METRIC fits, according to Learn?

options.text: COSINE, because IP isn't supported for vectors
options.why: IP is a supported metric. Learn limits it to pre-normalized or specialized models.
L2 is the guidance for image embeddings and spatial data.
Correct. Use IP only with pre-normalized embeddings or models that require it.
FLOAT64 is a data type, not a distance metric.

questions.hint: One metric is reserved for pre-normalized vectors.
questions.explain: COSINE: text embeddings. L2: image embeddings and spatial data. IP (inner product): only for pre-normalized embeddings or models that require it.

questions.q: How much memory does one 1,536-dimension FLOAT32 vector need?

options.why: Correct. 1,536 × 4 bytes ≈ 6 KB.
That's 384 dimensions.
That's far too large.
That's FLOAT64 at 8 bytes per dimension.

questions.hint: 4 bytes per value times 1,536 values.
questions.explain: FLOAT32 = 4 bytes per dimension; FLOAT64 = 8.

questions.q: A prototype searches 3,000 FAQ embeddings and needs exact results. Which algorithm fits?

options.why: DiskANN isn't one of Redis's algorithms here.
Correct. FLAT is exact and suits under 10,000 vectors.
HNSW is approximate and aimed at larger sets.
IVFFlat isn't one of Redis's algorithms in this module.

questions.hint: A few thousand vectors and exact results: brute force is fine.
questions.explain: Redis offers FLAT (exact) and HNSW (approximate).

questions.q: Match each workload to Learn's quick configuration guide.

items.text: Text search over a few thousand documents
Product recommendations across millions of items

questions.hint: Small text, large text, and images each have their own row in the guide.
questions.explain: Dataset size picks the algorithm; the embedding type picks the metric.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team proposes FLOAT64 for 10 million text embeddings "for better accuracy".

rows.text: FLOAT64 doubles vector memory compared with FLOAT32.
Learn says FLOAT64 gives meaningfully better accuracy for typical AI embeddings.
rows.why: The extra precision provides no meaningful improvement for nearly all AI applications.

rows.text: Larger vectors can also slow distance calculations.
rows.why: Larger data means more memory transfer.

questions.hint: Double the bytes, but no meaningful gain for embeddings.
questions.explain: Use FLOAT32 unless you need maximum precision for specialized research.

questions.q: With FLAT indexing, Learn's example gives about 10 ms for 10,000 vectors. Roughly how long might the same search take over 1 million vectors?

options.why: Correct. Learn's example: 1 million vectors could take around 1,000 ms.
FLAT time grows with dataset size.
That's ten times more than linear growth.
Linear growth from 10,000 to 1M is 100×.

questions.hint: Brute force grows in step with the number of vectors.
questions.explain: FLAT scales linearly; HNSW keeps queries fast on large datasets.

questions.q: A product recommendation engine must return similar items in under 10 milliseconds across several million product embeddings. A slightly imperfect top 10 is acceptable. Which algorithm fits?

options.why: Correct. HNSW gives near-instant results on millions of vectors by trading a little accuracy for speed.
FLAT compares every vector, which gets too slow at millions of items.
Searching without an index is brute force, which is the slow path.
A bigger data type makes brute force slower, not faster.

questions.hint: Millions of vectors and a strict latency budget call for approximate search.
questions.explain: FLAT guarantees exact results but slows linearly with dataset size. HNSW builds a multi-layer graph for near-instant search on millions of vectors with a small accuracy trade-off.

questions.q: A team switches to an embedding model that outputs 3,072 dimensions, but the Redis index was created with DIM 1536. What happens to similarity search?

options.text: The vectors don't match the index, because DIM must equal the model's output exactly
options.why: Correct. Distances compare position by position, so dimensions must match exactly.

options.text: Redis truncates the vectors to 1,536 values and searches normally
options.why: Redis doesn't adjust dimensions for you. Mismatched vectors don't work.

options.text: Redis expands the index to 3,072 dimensions on the first insert
options.why: DIM is fixed in the schema. You need a new index for the new model.

options.text: Search works, but returns approximate results
options.why: A dimension mismatch is a failure, not a lower-accuracy search.

questions.hint: Distance calculations line vectors up one position at a time.
questions.explain: Embedding models output fixed lengths (384, 768, 1024, 1536, 3072…). The index DIM must match the model's output exactly because distance calculations compare each dimension by position.

questions.q: Products have only flat fields (name, price, category) plus one embedding, and memory cost matters most. Which structure should you use?

options.why: Streams are for task queues.
Correct. Hash stores vectors as compact bytes with the lowest memory and fastest queries.
Lists aren't used for indexed vectors here.
JSON adds formatting overhead for flexibility you don't need.

questions.hint: Flat fields and lowest memory point to the simpler structure.
questions.explain: Hash for flat data and maximum performance; JSON when data is nested.

questions.q: Each product document has nested specs, several image URLs and two embeddings (title and image). Which structure fits best?

options.why: Splitting specs across keys loses the document structure.

options.text: A Hash with both embeddings concatenated
options.why: Concatenating vectors breaks dimension matching.
Correct. JSON handles nested structures and multiple vectors per item.
Separate strings lose the link to metadata and the index.

questions.hint: Nested specs and several embeddings fit a document structure.
questions.explain: Choose JSON for nested data and multiple vectors per item.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team stores vectors in Redis JSON documents.

rows.text: The embedding is stored as a numeric array, produced with tolist().
rows.why: JSON stores the vector as a JSON array.

rows.text: Index fields are referenced with JSONPath such as $.name and an as_name alias.
JSON uses less memory than Hash for the same vector.
rows.why: JSON adds array formatting overhead; Hash is lower.

questions.hint: JSON stores vectors as number lists and uses JSONPath. It isn't the smaller option.
questions.explain: JSON trades some memory and speed for flexibility.

questions.q: You're moving product vectors from Hash to JSON. Put the steps in order.
steps: Read each product from its Hash key
Convert it to a JSON document with the vector as a list
Write the JSON document to Redis
Delete the old index and create a new one with the JSON IndexType
questions.hint: Read the old data, convert, write, then rebuild the index for the new type.
questions.explain: Switching structures means re-ingesting data and recreating the index.

questions.q: 1 million flat product records with 1,536-dimension embeddings must give the lowest query latency and memory. A developer wants JSON "for future flexibility". What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Use both, storing every product twice
options.why: Storing everything twice wastes memory.

options.text: Use FLOAT64 in JSON to offset the extra overhead
options.why: FLOAT64 doubles memory and doesn't help.

options.text: Use Hash now; re-ingest into JSON later if needed
options.why: Correct. For simple metadata, Hash gives the best balance; switching later means re-ingesting.

options.text: Use JSON, because JSON queries vectors faster
options.why: Hash is faster than JSON.

questions.hint: Choose for today's needs. Migrating later is possible.
questions.explain: Hash saves significant memory and latency at this scale; use JSON when complexity requires it.

questions.q: You're storing a vector in a Redis Hash with the rest of a document's metadata. How should the embedding field be written, compared with storing it in a JSON document?

options.text: In a Hash, as a numeric list; in JSON, as bytes
options.why: That's the wrong way round.

options.text: In both, as a comma-separated string
options.why: Neither structure expects a text string of numbers.

options.text: In both, as bytes from tobytes()
options.why: JSON documents store the embedding as a numeric array.

options.text: In a Hash, as bytes from tobytes(); in JSON, as a numeric list from tolist()
options.why: Correct. Hash fields hold binary bytes, while JSON stores the vector as a numeric array.

questions.hint: Hashes store raw bytes, and JSON stores arrays.
questions.explain: With Hash, store embeddings as bytes (embedding.tobytes()) together with metadata via hset mapping. With JSON, store embeddings as numeric arrays (embedding.tolist()) and reference fields with JSONPath.
